Mr. Speaker, I rise to register my opposition to this particular resolution, and in doing so I may say that I speak only for myself. I do not know what position other hon. members of the house intend to take. For reasons which I shall elaborate I have had the particular act to which this resolution refers under consideration for some time. It is one of the acts which I heartily disapprove. It is one of several acts that were passed about the same time during the war. These acts in their very nature were emergency legislation, as will appear from the preamble to the original act which was passed in the fall of 1944 and which reads as follows:
Whereas it is desirable to promote the revival of trade by establishing a corporation to insure against loss caused by insolvency, delay in collection and transfer difficulties in connection with the export of Canadian-produced goods, and during the period of transition from war to peace by providing for loans or guarantees to governments of other countries or their agencies.
Surely three years after the war we can hardly say that we are in the period of transition from war to peace. In fact, as long ago as June, 1946, the government realized that the preamble was no longer applicable and repealed it, so that in the extensive amendments which were made in 1946 that preamble no longer appears because I presume the government considered it no longer applicable.
I cannot quite understand why this government should want to receive power to enter into any contracts that they have not the power to enter into at the present time because, as I read the act as it was enacted in 1946, they have power to enter into contracts to the extent of $200 million as to guarantees given to other countries, and to the extent of $750 million for the purchase of securities. Incidentally, the capital of the corporation is $10,000,000. These amounts seem to me to be considerable sums of money for one more or less innocuous corporation about which we have heard very little during the past few years. Perhaps one reason we have heard very

Export Credits Insurance Act
little about it is that very little publicity was given to the type of work that the corporation is doing.
As I understand it, the act is divided into two parts: loans to other governments and their agencies; and policies of insurance sold to exporters. In a return brought down to a question asked by me in February of this year, return No. 116A, it was stated that at the present time the bank had guaranteed $12,750,000 to three chartered banks in respect of credit given to the Ming Sing Industrial Company of China to purchase ships from Canada. So far as I know, that is the only guarantee given to another government agency, although the terms of the resolution may indicate that some larger guarantees are intended to be given.
I should like to say a word about the policies of insurance issued. Perhaps I should say this first, since the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in his opening statement referred to it. Apparently all the loans made to other countries under the amendment of 1946, which allowed the Dominion of Canada to extend credits to the extent of $750 million to countries other than the United Kingdom, were advanced under this act; therefore at the present time no responsibility rests upon the export credits corporation, because this money is a loan given to each country. Therefore there is no responsibility to be undertaken by the corporation; it has only to see that the money is properly handed over to a country and that the money is expended in Canada. It may be that up to the present time it had no great responsibility in that regard. One of the things I object to very much is the policies of insurance which the corporation is selling. Before the dinner recess the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) asked why private people could not issue these policies. The answer may be in the amendment that was made in 1946, but it does not seem to me a very compelling reason for the government to enter into a business which can be carried on privately in an economy that is supposed to be competitive. One of the amendments of the 1946 act says that the corporation may:
(a) for the purpose of facilitating and developing trade between Canada and any other country, enter into a contract of insurance with an exporter to insure hiim against any risk of loss in connection with the export or an agreement for the export of goods by reason of the failure of the exporter, for any cause not avoidable by the exporter, to recover the selling price of the goods.
That is a very practical guarantee. Certain exporters who buy one of these policies of 5849-1771
insurance will be guaranteed against loss which is not caused entirely by the negligence of the exporter. I presume he has to give some evidence of good faith and allow proper time to recover the money. Once before I asked a question about the reasons for these guarantees of insurance, and I know now why I have not received the answer. Therefore I have devised another way of trying to get some idea of the cost of these government agencies. In the return which I mentioned a while ago of February of this year, I received the following information: issued policies as of December 31. 1947, $23,964,827. I then asked a question as to the size of the policies, and the answer is as follows: one of $3,281,000; one of $2,550,000; one of $1,649,000; two of $1,000,000 each; one of $700,000; one of $580,000; one of $575,000, one of $550,000, and one of $500,000. Who are the fortunate people who received these policies of insurance because, as the minister stated in his opening remarks, goods were shipped all over the world? This is substantiated by the return of the corporation for the year 1947 which, incidentally, happened to come to us through the mail today. If the minister held off his resolution until this was available I want to thank him for doing so because we are in a little better position with that information. On an analysis of the countries of actual risks undertaken during the year 1947, I find a whole page. I think there are about sixty countries to which insurance guarantees have been given. The exports to foreign countries range from $1,000,000 to $3,300,000. Several had over $1,000,000. In the case of the United Kingdom the sum is $6,391,000. Therefore at different times there were guarantees to the extent of $28,000,000 given. Some have been repaid. In other words, guarantees are extended with respect to goods shipped to every part of the world. I cannot see why the government should be expected to give these guarantees and I believe that a considerable loss will be sustained in consequence.
The annual report for 1947 is somewhat better than that of the first nine months of 1946. It shows that the corporation had in their hands $10,000,000 advanced by the Dominion of Canada and on the amount they invested they received $196,000. They received $277,000 by way of premium on risks undertaken and their expenses were in the neighbourhood of $60,000, leaving a balance on hand of approximately $413,000, of which approximately $200,000 came from investments.
Now, $413,000 is just about four per cent on the money invested. If Canada is paying three per cent for money, and if, after this extensive trading in a year, there were no
Export Credits Insurance Act

actual losses last year, at least none being visible at the time of this return, the result is a surplus of 8122,000 to cover guarantees totalling at that time $23,000,000.
I do hot think that is good business. In my opinion the charge is far less than it should be. At one time I calculated it to be about one-fifth of one per cent, which is practically negligible so far as the exporters are concerned. Anyone can appreciate that even if there is not a loss at all it becomes a small charge to the exporter. I-fear, therefore, the people of Canada will suffer a great loss.
I realize that the directors are all government employees. The act- made provision for certain others to be appointed; but, apart from the general manager, the directors are all employees in the higher brackets either of the government or of the Bank of Canada. There is also an advisory council. I have nothing to say against the advisory council, which is composed of men of substance in the community, but I doubt whether these men have the time to look into many of these different transactions which this government is bound to investigate during the course of the year. I suggest that they can deal intelligently only with certain ones about which they have some knowledge, and the ones they know of would be corporations that would not require the assistance of the government, because they could make use of the insurance companies now available throughout Canada.
I object strenuously to this as I do to three or four other corporations of the kind, for the reason that we do not know what they are doing. We do not know who is borrowing money. The minister intimated, I gathered, that a list of the loans will be available to members of parliament. That will be in the future, because I do not believe that any member has seen it in the past. But I submit that making the list accessible under conditions of secrecy will not serve any useful purpose, because in that case, one may say too much, and then it will no longer be secret, or, if strict secrecy is observed, the information obtained will be of no value to the person who gets it. The information should be available to everyone.
It may be that these exporters do not want their business known. If they do not, they should not apply for the guarantee. They must take the consequence of asking for something which no one else will give them at a reasonable premium.
In regard to this particular corporation, I take the same position that I take with respect to any other department of government. I suggest that a minister of the crown or a

deputy minister should always stand on guard in his relations to friends or to other people who may have a persuasive manner, and1 if he has the knowledge that the people of Canada will learn of the transaction it will make it easier to say " no." I do not think any man seeking a favour would dare to ask for it if he knew he did not deserve it, and that the public would learn of the transaction.
I do not say that, in the matter of publicity, the facts need be widely publicized:, but the information should1 be available to everyone; otherwise it is not democratic. If it is a case where only seven, eight, nine or ten people know the facts in Canada, you have no democracy. In a dictatorship only one man knows, but the difference is merely that in one case ten men are dictators and in the other only one man is. I do not think that is in keeping with democratic government, and I do not believe the exporters of Canada, with their reputation for shrewdness and for sound1 trading, need be coddled by the government. They should stand on their own feet; otherwise the weaker ones will be in the same position as the strong ones. We do not want ambassadors all over the world. We want live trade commissioners who will look after the trade of Canada. For these reasons I am opposed to the resolution carrying.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Golding in the chair.

In the report of the corporation I do not see anything by way of reserve on account of outstanding policies in the assets and liabilities. I should like to ask the minister why the premiums were not disclosed before and why they are to be disclosed now. I should also like to know what losses have been sustained so far. What reserve is set up for outstanding policies?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: If my hon. friend will read the statement distributed for the year ended December 31, 1947, he will find that at the end of that year the reserve had been built up to $584,336.07. The capital of $10,000,000 which was credited to the corporation on its formation is still intact.

On what basis are the reserves arrived at? The outstanding liabilities must be very large. I believe the outstanding liabilities under policies outstanding are $27,000,000 and it does not seem to me that $584,000 is sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Reserves can be built up only from earnings. We have the $10,000,000 capital.

Export Credits Insurance Act
Reserves are a different thing from surplus. I am talking about reserves.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The surplus that my hon. friend talks about is built up from earnings just as the reserves are built up from earnings.
Excuse me; you have two different things. One is reserves and the other is premiums.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: All the premiums received to date are in the underwriting reserve.
What reserves have you on account of losses which will take place, out of this 827,000,000? All you have is something like $485,000.

speechtext: You have $584,336.07 along with the original capital of $10,000,000 invested in the company.
Can the minister give us some idea about how these reserves are arrived at?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: These reserves are the total earnings of the company, the total receipts from premiums less the cost of operating the company.

I do not think that is correct. The minister has the two things mixed up. First of all, you have a surplus which is a different thing altogether. What you have, as a matter of fact, and what you must have are reserves on account of unearned premiums. What are those reserves on account of unearned premiums? What is the basis of arriving at those reserves?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Call them what you will, everything that has been paid into the company is in the form of reserves as shown in the statement. That is all the money there is, and there is not any more. This company was given $10,000,000 when it started and it has collected $584,000 more than it has paid out in operating expenses. That is all the money there is. How can my hon. friend find reserves beyond that point?

I do not think the minister gets the idea yet. You have outstanding liabilities of something like $27,000,000. That is what you have. What reserve have you against these outstanding liabilities? What reserves do you put up? How do you arrive at the reserves which must be put up there?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I arrive at the reserves by adding the capital and the earnings, and that is all the money there is.

I am trying to get at it from a different point of view. Your capital and what you have earned and so on constitute your surplus. But out of this $27,000,000 you will have some losses. What do you expect to have by way of losses and what reserve do you set up under this for those losses? That is what I want to get at, and I do not see it in the statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I will read from the annual report:
The financial statements of the corporation show that an underwriting .reserve of $584,336.07 has been accumulated. Since the business of the corporation is to protect exporters against credit and political risks involved in foreign trade, it must be expected that there will be an appreciable loss experience over a period of years. The three years of the corporation's existence cannot be regarded as typical in this respect mainly because of the favourable credit conditions during this period. Accordingly, while no specific provision has been made for anticipated losses, the total excess of income over expenditure since the commencement of the corpora; tion's operations has been credited to the underwriting reserve.

I still do not think the minister gets the point. I understand what he has. For instance, you have here the excess of income over expenditures for the year ended December 31,	1947, which is
$422,000. That is what your excess of income over expenditure is. 1 understand that all right. But what anticipated losses have you? This statement does not tell me that. What anticipated losses will there be? What do you put in your statement here by way of a reserve for that? For instance, with regard to ordinary year by year fire insurance, the department of insurance in Canada requires that 40 per cent must be put up on your unearned premiums by wray of reserve against anticipated losses. Where does that come-into this statement? That is what I am trying to get at. What do you expect to have-by way of losses out of this $27,000,000? That, is the only way we can tell about this.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The inspector of insurance is satisfied with 40 per cent of the premiums as a loss reserve. We are taking 100 per cent.of the premiums. Surely we are being more conservative than the company my hon. friend is telling us about. All we can do is put all the money we earn into an insurance reserve.
Yes, I agree with you. You put it in the reserve. But w'hat do you anticipate your losses will be?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
We have had no losses to date. We have had a limited experience, but we have had no losses.
Export Credits Insurance Act

That is what I want to get at. How do you know your premiums are adequate for the risk you take? Or do you figure that the government of Canada will pay those losses anyway? Do you figure that we shall pay them anyway whether we get the premiums or not?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
No, Mr. Chairman-
No. I want an answer to my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply

speechtext: I just want to ask one other question which I asked before. Why should the rates of premiums on policies of this kind be cheaper, and why are you not to have them open for inspection now? What is the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: They differ between the different countries. They have some relation to the political risk involved. Naturally, we do not want all countries to compare their position in this insurance fund with that of others. There are obvious reasons why we do not publish rates. We like to look at the risk, decide whether we want it or not and, if we want it, the rate of insurance that we shall charge, just as any insurance company would do.
Are these policies which are being issued at the present time annual policies or for a period of time?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We issue both types; we issue annual policies to cover general commodities and also capital goods policies to cover a particular risk. For example, if we are selling a ship paid for by progress payments, the policy will extend over the life of the liability.

I do not propose to delay the committee to any

extent now, but I should like to raise one or two points which I think should be gone into with considerable care when we come to the committee stage of the bill. When the Speaker was in the chair this afternoon the minister said, as I understood him, that the reason the public corporation was dealing with these risks was that private business could not take them on. Am I correct in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.

I have seen the report since this afternoon, and I have been studying it. Unless the ordinr ary insurers have changed their whole way of doing business, or want to go out of business altogether, it is hard for me to understand why they cannot take risks in Australia, let us say, or the United Kingdom, or the Netherlands, and I could mention some other countries. The minister has spoken about political risks. If people were shipping goods to Czechoslovakia or Hungary or Poland I can understand that there might be great political risks; but when we reach the committee stage on the bill I think perhaps the minister might give us some indication of what he bases his opinion on that this must be done by a government agency, and why no private corporation will undertake it. I propose to try to find out something more about that myself. In passing, I notice that we have guaranteed over a million dollars going to the United States of America. If I am correct in thinking that political risks enter into this and, while not the whole, form a large part of the reason for government intervention, surely the United States should not be included.
I do not want to take more time on this now. If the minister thinks it would be better to deal with these matters when we are in the committee stage on the bill, I am content; but it seems to me that we would require some evidence, let us say, far beyond anything I have read, that in the case of many of these countries private business has thrown up its hands, so we have to do this through a public agency.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
It is a fact that there are no companies insuring export credits to any country except the United States. That is the fact, but I cannot say why. We wish they were, because wre do not particularly like this business; but there are risks today in shipping to almost any country, outside the United States, which risks a private firm cannot assess. There is the risk of devaluation of the currency; the risk of blockage of funds, and various risks of that kind which are peculiar to this period, which the government can assess

Dominion Elections Act
and probably work out, but on which no private firm could possibly take a chance.
Of course, wherever those conditions exist I can see the reason for it; but does the minister apply those words- "risk of a sudden blockage of funds," for instance-to the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Certainly.

In spite of the over-all financial arrangements we have, does the minister mean that a private firm could not satisfy itself, in making a deal in the United Kingdom, that it might not suddenly find the funds blocked?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The fact is that, out of $28,000,000 of outstanding policies, over $6,000,000 are in the United Kingdom. As a matter of fact we have been approached for very large policies with respect to the United Kingdom, policies we could not take on because they would throw our whole insurance plan out of balance. But it is also a fact that many exporters, even though they are exporting through channels they may know all about, believe it is worth the price of a policy just to get the Canadian government behind their risk.

I am not going to pursue the matter further now, but frankly I am still puzzled. When the matter comes up again I may know more about it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER

speechtext:
Hon. COLIN GIBSON (Secretary of State) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Dominion Elections Act, 1938, to make provision inter alia for an increase of salary to the chief electoral officer.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Golding in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Some years ago I suggested the salary of the chief electoral officer should be increased, and at the time the circumstances were particularly interesting. There were two men. One was doing nothing and was receiving $10,000 a year. The other, the present chief electoral officer, was receiving only $4,000 and was doing all the work. This seemed strange and I suggested that the $10,000 should be given the man who was working hard and that the other gentleman should be given no more than $4,000. There was a compromise, and the chief electoral officer was paid $8,000.
He is doing splendid work, and I hope that some day a journalist will ask him for an interview and learn how he succeeded in having the ballots returned on time from all parts of the country after the last election.
It was quite an accomplishment, and he deserves special recognition for that. I know he is helped by his son, who has a very fine war record; and I also hope that the services -rendered by his son will be recognized in due course.
I am an old timer, Mr. Chairman; I remember elections when the electoral officials were .much better paid than they are now, at a time when money had more value than it has today. We are now at the resolution stage of this matter, and I hope that the minister will be good enough to look into the past and see what wras formerly paid in both urban and rural centres for the polling booths and to the returning officers, the deputy returning officers, the clerks and all the others who have to do with an election. I remember that in my first election a constable was at the door of every polling booth. That is a good thing; it inspires respect for justice on the part of everyone, even those who are not telegraphers. There are no such people in my constituency, but I speak now of the large, urban centres. In those days the rental paid for the polling booth was much higher than is now the case; and I suggest to the director of elections that all those in this country engaged in electoral work should be at least, as well rewarded now as they were twenty or twenty-five years ago. There is no reason why they should not be. And if the salary of the chief electoral officer is to be adjusted now-and I am for it-the salaries of all those engaged in elections work by the government should go up to the level they were twenty or twenty-five years ago. You know, sir, that the whole thing has been decreased gradually and that no one has noticed it. There are many new members who appear for the first time. They do not pay much attention to the amount paid to
Dominion Elections Act

these men. It is most important to reward them well, because they are doing their duty. If we want to have good men we have to pay them a reasonable amount for the time they spend on public business to help the country in the proper carrying out of elections. The minister must know that. He is not a newcomer but has been in the house for some time.
I was here before the minister came, and I remember the happy time when the adjustment of those salaries was more just than it is now. I shall not insist further, but I will ask for a complete tabulation of the amounts paid to all the electoral officers and for the renting of the polls at the present time and twenty or twenty-five years ago. I shall not ask for all the changes in the statute; that might take too much space in Hansard. I hope that the minister will accept my most reasonable request, which is made on behalf of thousands of people across the country.

I am not going to debate the question at all, but I just wish to ask the minister why this matter is again referred to the committee when the committee appointed last year made an exhaustive study of the elections act and presented its report to parliament. I should hope that if there is nothing new the committee would not have to go over the same ground again.
The matter mentioned in the resolution, namely the increase in the salary of the chief electoral officer, was dealt with in the committee's report of last year. Before taking my seat, may I associate myself with what was said by the hon. member for Temiscouata with respect to the chief electoral officer. He is, I think, one of Canada's most respected servants, and certainly I did not have any objection last year to increasing the salary, nor will I have any this year. But I should like to know just why this matter is again referred to a committee in view of the exhaustive study given the matter last year.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER

As the hon. member has stated, this bill was referred to a committee at the last session of parliament. That committee reported, but the bill was not reached before the session ended. In the interval between sessions the chief electoral officer has come across some minor amendments he feels should be made, and he has several further suggestions to offer. It was considered advisable to have a committee consisting of the same personnel as at the last session study these suggestions before the bill receives second reading. I have on the order paper a notice for the setting up of that committee. Hon. members will see that, with two

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER

I should like to ask one question relating to a matter which might be dealt with by way of study on the part of the chief electoral officer, might be studied by the committee the minister proposes to set up, or might be studied by the government itself. I refer to the question of arranging for having redistribution carried out by some body other than the House of Commons. When I raised this matter last year one of the chief objections put forward by the hon. member for Quebec South was that the issue was too much alive at that time to permit the time being taken up which would be necessary in order to work out proper legislation. The hon. member for Quebec South told the house that at a previous time, I believe when he was Postmaster General, he had had charge of preparing a bill to permit redistribution to be done by an independent commission.
When this question of an independent commission is raised when redistribution is actually being effected I realize that the argument can be brought forth that there is not time to do it. In other words, the time to reconsider the whole position is in the lull between redistributions. As the Secretary of State knows, we in Canada are backward in this respect. Most democratic countries, such as the United Kingdom, New Zealand, Australia and South Africa, do it the other way. It is not the issue now that it was last year when we had a redistribution bill before the house, but it is a matter related to the elections act and I believe it would come under the supervision of the Secretary of State. My hon. friend should be the last man to quote the hon. member for Lake Centre because they never agree on anything. I will not insist too much on it because I believe in the intelligence of my colleagues and I bow to their pride as faithful members of parliament. I am so sure of what I say that I would have no objection to having the limits of my constituency not changed perhaps but supervised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. If he changed it, if he made my county smaller or larger it would make no difference to me because they are all my friends. He is too practical to waste his time on that, but I will tell him something more. Leaving aside all political considerations, I do not know whether my hon. friend is familiar with the parish organizations in the province of Quebec. It must be the same in the other provinces. I have been there occasionally, but I have not lived long enough in any other province to be able to express a definite opinion on it.
There is the parish, which is a unit. It is a complete unit. People live together, and they have some tradesmen and some farmers. To a certain extent they are self-sufficient. Then the assemblies of these units that are the parishes of the county form the county itself.
There are particular boundaries between those who are within that unit. There may be wholesalers and others and the railway facilities. They join together and they go there. My idea of a redistribution is to respect and conserve these two units as much as possible and not pass the boundary of a constituency through the middle of a parish, not take a parish that has been for a long time within a county and put it somewhere else, but respect the customs and traditions of the people.
When some people are taken away from a constituency where their families have been living for a long time it creates a disturbance in their minds; it annoys them, and it causes them difficulties in their daily relations with the other people. The Canadian people have enough grounds for complaint without putting them in front of a judge who will be more compromising than anybody to create trouble. He will try to appease everybody. It will be the same thing as in Russia. The Russians have got everything by blackmail. There will be in front of a judge a party who will insist on having something unjust and create trouble by persistence. Then the judge will say, "Well, we will try to appease him"; and he will give him a slice of the other county to which he is not entitled. These are considerations with which everyone is familiar in the province of Quebec. I am sorry that my hon. friends of the west do not know so much about it; but if they come some day they will have only to let me know and I shall be glad to drive them around and show them that beautiful part of the country.
In cities it is different; there are not the same ties between people. People live in the same house and they do not know each other, but in the country it is hard to make a division like that. The ties are not so strong in large cities. Then there are certain traditions. There are people who do not know each other who sometimes go to the same store or send their children to a certain school, and when there are changes in constituencies it embarrasses them very much. All I shall pray for is that the wisdom of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will be just as useful to him as he wants it to be to others.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIDLE INCOMES, ETC.

speechtext:
Hon. MILTON F. GREGG (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved the second reading of Bill No. 196, to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1946.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in presenting this bill for second reading I should like to make a few general remarks. At present and for some time to come, the benefits relating to this bill will apply in the main to a small proportion of the oldi soldiers of the first great war.
In recent times my department, this house and the country as a whole have been giving, and quite property so, a great deal of attention to the needs of rehabilitation for the young veteran, and I should like to grasp this chance tonight to say a word on behalf of the smaller group of old-timers, contemporaries if you like of a good many of the veterans of the old war who are members of this house.

TFar Veterans Allowance Act
In the war of 1914-18 Canada had a total of approximately 646,000 men in the' armed forces, mainly in the army, a small group in the Canadian navy, and also a small group, serving under command, with the old Royal Flying Corps, of the British.
As closely as can be checked, that old 1914-18 armed force was distributed something like this: engaged in a theatre of war, which for the old war army was confined to the continent of Europe; for the navy, on or under the sea, and for the air force, the Royal Flying Corps, a total of 353,000; a total on service, but not so defined as engaged in a theatre of war, of approximately 293,000.
The War Veterans Allowance Act, to which this bill refers, applies mainly to the first group that I have mentioned. In it I said there were about 353,000. There is no means of telling exactly how many of them have survived the thirty years since their demobilization; but, as closely as can be learned, the figure today is in the vicinity of 200,000 survivors who took part in the fighting or in the theatre of operations in 1914-18, upon the sea, on the long land trail from Ypres to Mons, and with the Royal Flying Corps when flying was in its infancy, and when to go into the air in one of the old crates was in itself a hazard.
What has happened during the past thirty years to these men who were engaged in a theatre of war? After 1919 they set about the task of becoming Canadian citizens, and it was not too easy a one. They received little help compared with the new veterans; yet they were and still are the most forceful and effective sponsors of a better chance for the new veterans. I should like to emphasize the fact that, as far as I know, not one of the old-timers has ever raised a jealous voice in that regard. On the whole they have become valuable, productive Canadian citizens. They are Canadian citizens first, last and all the time. Many of them are leaders in various walks of our Canadian life. They spurned all temptations to carry over into the peace a solid ex-soldier group, politically or otherwise, and they have stood firmly down through the years against any temptation to demand money from their country purely on the basis of services rendered.
What is the picture regarding the whole 200,000 of those who fought and who have not yet died? Of those 200,000, all but approximately 25,000 are carrying on as Canadian citizens without any aid from their country, other than compensation for some honourable war disabilities which they still carry. A little
over 25,000 men therefore who, under our definition, saw battle service are at the moment in receipt of war veterans allowance. Their numbers, by the very nature of things, as they move on to the sixty, sixty-five and seventy age group, are bound to increase for the next ten years at least.
Hon. members are aware, I know, of the history of the War Veterans Allowance Act upon which this bill is based. In it our country attempted to see to it that this small portion of the 1914-18 force'-as it stands now only about five per cent of the total force-should not beg on the streets. Through old age, through premature aging due to battle strain or fatigue, through physical disabilities not pensionable, through hard luck and a score of other reasons beyond their control, they are unable to cope with life in full measure. Some of them remained bachelors. An extraordinarily large number did so; as far as we can record, the number was approximately 12,000. A total of approximately 13,000 married. And with nearly all of them who married, by the very nature of things children have grown up and have now gone away.
These men all gave honourable fighting service to Canada and they should be ensured an honourable old age. For those, and for others who may yet qualify, this bill proposes more generous terms. I should like to interject here that it is only as a very last resort that these older veterans will accept aid under this act. They prefer to earn their own living just so long as work within their capacity can be found.
It is not too easy in these days of streamlined industry to keep the employment door open to men of their age. With good support from employers of labour, the good offices of the corps of commissionaires, and services set up jointly with the placement service of the Department of Labour, over 100,000 veterans of world war I have been rendered employment services since April 1, 1946, when that service really got under way in the Department of Veterans Affairs. This will to work has had its influence on expenditures under the act. Many have been enabled to give up the allowance voluntarily and a large number now happily and gainfully employed would otherwise have been a charge upon the country.
Hon. members might like to have a general outline of present war veterans allowance beneficiaries and costs. The War Veterans Allowance Act came into operation in Sep-

In addition to the matter of increase, this bill rearranges what was known as "casual earnings" and raises the ceiling of permissible income under the act to $1,105 a year, or approximately $92 a month for married men and to $615 a year, or approximately $51 a month for single mem. It is the intention to use the supplementary allowance to augment the recipient's income under these new ceilings. This will result in a flat increase to all recipients in an amount not exceeding $10 a month, made possible by the raising of the ceiling on permissible income.
For the purpose of dealing with the increases, recipients of the war veterans allowance will be divided into three classes by the department in working it out. Some 6,303 pensioners now in receipt of war veterans allowance will have their increase in the war veterans allowance, as well as the pension increase. Of this number, there are 3,702 married men receiving up to 60 per cent pension and 2,601 single men receiving up to 50 per cent pension. In the second class there are now 16,711 non-pensioners who are at present receiving the maximum war veterans allowance and who have no other income; and they will receive the full supplementary allowance. In the third class there are 10,284 additional recipients, also non-pensioners, who are not in receipt of the maximum war veterans allowance. They may have their allowance adjusted under the new ceiling.
It will be noted that in this bill there is the same amount of increase for both married and single recipients, that is, $10 a month in each

case. In the original act the scale was $40 for a married man and $20 for a single man. I think it was pretty well an arbitrary arrangement, that the married man should get twice as much as the single man, though I do not know what the plan was. During the last war, authority was given, based on need, to increase this scale to $60 for a married man and $30 for a single man, and when the act was amended in 1946 these became the new rates. It has been considered that in this there is some degree of inequity as between the rates for single and married men. In no other veteran legislation are man and wife together paid twice the amount paid a single man; and now that a further increase is planned it seems that this inequity might be corrected.
Let me briefly review some examples. Under the proposed pension rates a 100 per cent pensioner, married, will receive $117 a month; a 100 per cent pensioner, single, will receive $87 a month. Married veteran students now receive $90 a month; single veteran students receive $60. Married veterans awaiting returns, unemployed or temporarily incapacitated receive $70 a month; single veterans receive $50. It is suggested here that the time has arrived when the war veterans allowances, married and single rates, should be brought into some conformity with the other rates I have just indicated. Consequently the new rate proposed here is $70 a month for the married veteran and $40 a month for the single veteran.
The terms of this bill, will, I anticipate, receive careful study by the special committee on veterans affairs. In the main, Mr. Speaker, this bill is a further important step toward giving the old soldier who fought for his country the assurance that in his old age his country will provide him with some defence against poverty.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIDLE INCOMES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened with interest to the speech of the minister and his recital of the history of the war veterans allowance. First let me say I agree that in the period since the war the young soldier should have been given the greatest attention, and as we know that has been done. As the minister has said, the older soldier made no complaint in that regard; he was only too anxious to assist. As a matter of fact I think the old soldier in Canada can be complimented, not only on his attitude during and since the second war, but also on his attitude since the first war. The Canadian soldier has never been very demanding of the Canadian people. When the attitude of our soldiers is compared with that of soldiers of other countries-and I might particularly mention the attitude of returned soldiers in the

War Veterans Allowance Act
country to the south of us-I believe our returned soldiers are to be highly commended. I remember that a few years ago, for instance, some of the returned soldiers in the United States marched on the capital of that country, demanding a bonus which ran into many millions of dollars.
Since the resolution preceding this bill was introduced, we have had an opportunity to review the legislation. At the outset may I say that personally I have found it disappointing, and I am satisfied that is the reaction of many hon. members. It does not contain what we expected it would. It is true that it mentions the matters of which the minister has spoken; and while we are not allowed, nor do I intend, to take it up section by section, we have certain small amendments, like the one concerning deserted children, which have something of an emotional appeal but really do not amount to very much as far as dollars and cents are concerned. There would be very few deserted children of soldiers in receipt of the veterans allowance, and I should imagine the provision in that section would cost very little. If we go on to the next section we see that it provides for an increase in the salaries of members of the pension board. I see you are stirring, Mr. Speaker. I do not intend to deal with the sections individually, I am simply pointing out that some provisions of the bill are really not very important as far as the old soldier is concerned, about whose welfare the minister said tonight we were very anxious.
This legislation is going to the committee on veterans affairs, where it will be thoroughly discussed; there need be no doubt of that. I am sorry the bill does not contain more, because I feel that in other bills which have gone to the veterans affairs committee we have been, as it were, too circumscribed in our discussion of such legislation, and this bill is just another example. It contains too little; and the committee cannot make amendments, which I am satisfied we would feel like making, in providing benefits for our old soldiers.
The minister has told us about the history of the War Veterans Allowance Act. May I say at the outset that I have always considered it one of the finest acts, so far as veterans legislation is concerned. This act was brought into force in 1930, eighteen years ago. It was considered then that there were many veterans in this country who were unable to take their place in the labour market of the country and who, indeed, were entitled to assistance.
In 1930 the veterans under the War Veterans Allowance Act were given $20 a month. That
was, of course, a small sum, but it compared at that time with the Old Age Pensions Act, of which it was more or less a supplement so far as the soldier was concerned. As the minister pointed out, it has been increased to $30 a month; and now, under certain conditions, the veteran is to receive $40 a month.
In the minister's solicitation for the old soldiers of this country, I felt that Bill No. 196 should have been larger in its scope and should have given benefits to classes of old soldiers other than those mentioned in the bill. For instance, for many years in the house and in committee there has been one group of soldiers for the inclusion of which the Canadian Legion and other Canadian organizations have strongly urged. I refer to those soldiers who in the last war did not get any farther than England. To my mind those men should receive consideration and attention in this bill. I am expressing not only my own opinion, but the opinion of war veterans organizations in this country for many years. There are not many of these men, and the country would not be bankrupted if we included those men who served only in England in the last war. An estimate made in the veterans committee in 1946 placed the amount at less than $3,000,000 that it would cost the country.
In this connection I should like to read a letter I received only a few weeks ago. May I add that the letter comes from a constituent of the minister? This old soldier writes to me in these words:
Please excuse my writing you, but I note in the Legionary that the legion is again going to plead the case of the vets who only got as far as England in world war I before the parliamentary committee, so I thought I would like to state to you my case. First. I was R.S.M. No. 1 of the 13th New Brunswick reserve battalion. I applied to Colonel Fowler to be allowed to go to France, and his reply was. "No, you are too much value to me." When Major Stirling took over I .again applied, but the answer was the same. He went so far as to say they could get lots of men to go to France, but not to take my place. Colonel A. L. Barry now in the fisheries department. Ottawa, can and will vouch for this. I am barred from getting the war veterans allowance. Yet others who were in France but a day or two and saw no action are eligible. Hardly fair. I think. I trained and prepared hundreds of men for their job in the service.
I am seventy-nine years of age, cannot work and have to live on $20 British army pension and $30 old age pension per month, and pay $10 per month rent. Tough going.
I am not ashing you to do anything for me, but thought I would like to write you and to state my case, as it might be helpful to others.
The point this old soldier brings out is that he enlisted, went to England, served as a sergeant-major over there and was not allowed to go to France as he had wished. Now, when
War Veterans Allowance Act

he is an old man, he is barred from receiving war veterans allowance. I know; I am sure the minister knows, and every soldier member in the house knows that there were thousands of men who went to France and who have no more front-line service than did these men in England. Yet the fact that they sailed across twenty-two miles of water makes them today eligible for war veterans allowance, while these other men who, for no reason of their own, were compelled to stay in England, do not receive it. I say that is a grave injustice and one which I personally had hoped would be corrected in the bill which we have before us tonight.
There is another class of men whom I should like to mention, and who, I hoped, would be included. These are the imperials, the men who served from 1914 to 1916 in the same war in which we served, men who fought for the same things for which we were fighting, men who, if they had not given service, might have brought about a condition whereby more men from this country would have had to sacrifice their lives. Those men came to Canada and made their homes here. For many years they helped to build this country.
In the last war they served Canada again, as did also their sons and daughters. Yet those men who in the last war served alongside Canadian soldiers, and whose sons and daughters served alongside Canadian soldiers in the last war, are not included in the bill and do not receive the benefits of war veterans allowances. I claim this is most unfair.
A few minutes ago I said this was not my own idea. I should like to read to the house some recommendations which were made by the Canadian Legion. This one was made in 1945:
Be it resolved that the War Veterans Allowance Act be so amended that the same privileges and assistance may be granted to veterans who enlisted in the Canadian expeditionary force and served outside of Canada as are now granted to men who served in an actual theatre of war within the meaning of War Veterans Allowance Act.
That would mean the men who had served in England in the last war. The resolution referring to imperial veterans is as follows:
Be it resolved that we endorse the present policy of the legion which has been aforestated as follows:
"That we urge upon the dominion government action to extend the war veterans allowance to ex-imperial veterans under the same conditions as to Canadian veterans, other than on the question of pre-war domicile, providing such imperial ex-service men were resident in Canada on September 1, 1930, and have since resided in Canada or who may have had continuous residence in Canada for a period of 20 years."

That is, they recommend that imperial veterans who were in Canada in 1930, the date on which the War Veterans Allowance Act was passed, be included in the act, if they also served in the Canadian army during the last war. Surely that is a most reasonable request.
The cost of this was brought out in the veterans committee in 1946, at which time it was shown that the cost of including these imperial veterans would be in the vicinity of Sl,900,000. That is not a tremendous amount of money, as we think of money today. Why, one of the members of the cabinet not so long ago said that a million dollars does not amount to anything. So I say we could very well afford to give these men this consideration.
The war veterans allowance has come to be regarded as a social security measure for veterans and the distinctions that have been made are distasteful. Many of these men fought side by side in the same cause. There are Canadians who served in both world wars but who did not go overseas and who are now eligible for what was hitherto known as the veterans dual service pension. There seems to be no good reason for excluding the imperial veteran of the first world war who served with the Canadian forces in Canada in the second world war. Many men served with the Canadian forces in theatres of operation in the second world war, and if we excluded the imperial first world war veteran who served with the Canadian forces in the second world war we would be discriminating as between men who served side by side in the Canadian forces under exactly the same conditions.
There are other implications of these regulations. The widow of the Canadian soldier who served only in England during the last war is excluded from receiving benefits under war veterans allowances, and there are many hundreds of these widows in Canada. They see the widow of some other soldier receiving benefits. They realize that their husbands served where they were told to serve. Any man in the army goes where he is told to go and serves where he is told to serve, in Canada, in England, or wherever it may be. I say it is unfair that these women should not have the benefits of the war veterans allowances. The same thing applies to widows of members of the imperial forces.
These are the main points that I wish to bring up tonight. I approve the supplementary allowance of $120 a year, but here again there is a nigger in the woodpile. We find that a man must undergo a means test if he is to receive this increase of $10 a month. I contend that if a man is entitled to a war veterans allowance,

War Veterans Allowance Act
if he has had his first means test, then there should be no further means test as far as he is concerned.
There is a bad moral effect. You may have two men each receiving war veterans allowances. One man may not be inclined to work; he is lazy and indifferent. He is not thrifty and does not try to improve his situation, but he is eligible for the increase from $30 to $40 a month. Then you have a man who is thrifty, who wants to work and help himself. I am sure we are all disposed to encourage that type of man. If this man works hard he may be deprived of the benefits of the war veterans allowance.
I contend that that is a great flaw in our veterans legislation. It should be so drawn as to encourage the thrifty and hardworking man and not to encourage the man who is slothful, lazy and indigent. This legislation encourages men to lie about their conditions, to conceal the facts. Unfortunately the same thing is true in connection with old age pensions. I will not say all, but because of the means test some of the older people in this country who wish to improve their condition find that they must tell some white lies about their financial position. I know my colleagues on this side and probably those on the other side will wish to discuss the matter very fully. speechtext:
Yes. Like the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), we are unable to understand why we cannot re-define the word "veteran" in the act. During the 1945 and 1946 sessions of the special parliamentary committee, we had quite a lot of discussion as to what should be actually a theatre of war. Britain is actually one of those theatres. I see no reason why the veterans of world war I who served in Britain during that time, but *who were subject to be sent to any theatre of action, should not be included. And I say that, having been one of those who did not remain in Britain. I went along in the mud. We believe that the act should be rewritten, so that for world war I Britain would be written into the definition of a theatre of war. This would include a lot of .people, but they are people who are extremely deserving citizens and veterans in this country. I believe the minister should give serious consideration to accepting that recommendation either here or in committee.
Again the hon. member for Royal brought up another class of veterans who are not very numerous in this country but who are certainly very deserving of all the benefits any veteran has in this country. I refer to those who served in the imperial forces but did not have the residence, or were not domiciled in Canada prior to their enlistment in the imperial forces. These people came over after the war and settled here in some industry or work
(Mr. Bentley.]
or in business or on farms. They became part of the community and likely are citizens now. Probably they have families here as well as interests. They are going to stay here. We of this group believe that they should be included in all the benefits, and that section or provision which requires that they should have been domiciled here before enlistment should be struck out and those citizens treated as they should be.
Another thing that I find it difficult to understand, and people with whom I have talked have told me that they find the same difficulty, has to do with those who have not yet reached the age of sixty so far as men are concerned and fifty-five so far as women are concerned, which the act requires. Generally, although there is a provision in the act that the war veterans allowance board may look sympathetically on claims of people who are below that age but otherwise qualified, we believe it should be more generous, and we believe that the treasury board should not only permit but encourage the war veterans allowance board to be more generous with these people who are not yet of the age but who are incapacitated for some reason or another, burnt out, before they reach the limit of age in the act.
Next is something that we have had many debates on since I have been here and have tried to prevent. That is the cost of living which has gone up tremendously, but at no time has the allowance paid to war veterans been large enough to take care of their needs and keep them in comfort. It has been a bare existence under any circumstances. I believe it was not until the war that it was even increased by order in council from $20 to the $30 that it is now and eventually worked into the statute by legislation. We believe at the present time that, because of the high cost of living, the allowance should be increased, not by the amount mentioned in section 8 of the amendment but to $50 a month for a single veteran, with a corresponding increase for a married veteran. We see no reason why a veteran who has had the misfortune that the minister speaks about-I believe the description he gave of what happened to some of them was just plain hard luck-and is burnt out should be in any different position from that of one who was actually burnt out or disabled because of war services. I say that because these veterans are just as needy and require just as much comfort, care and security as the ones who were disabled by war conditions or by war action. Therefore we believe that the allowance should be raised. I do not think it would cause a great strain on the treasury board and break their purse-

War Veterans Allowance Act
strings entirely. I believe this country can afford it a lot better than it can afford some of the things which will be carried on over the next year by our government unless, of course, they give us an opportunity to defeat them this summer some time, which I hope they do.
I should like to mention something else, which is not mentioned in the amendment. In the original act, and very largely in this bill, besides his actual amount of 8365 a year a veteran is allowed to have an income of $125 from some sources, casual earnings of $125 if he can earn them, and an investment earning of $25. I see no reason why the incomes from these sources should be specified as coming from different sources. Why not say that he can have it from any source up to a certain amount if we are to continue to apply the means test which, incidentally, I do not believe in; but I know it is there and is likely to remain? WTe believe that all these various sources of income should be grouped in the amount that he is allowed, and whether he gets it from interest on a war bond or from rentals from some little property he may happen to own or whether he earns it, or by whatever means he happens to get it, it should be in the aggregate and not specified in different amounts.
Another matter that is not dealt with here- and I am surprised that it has not been given consideration by the government, by the minister and by his officers-is the case of a veteran who qualifies in every respect for a war veterans allowance, but who has not lived in Canada for three months prior to the decision to grant him one. A burnt-out veteran is just as badly off if he lives in Arizona or in Iowa as if he lives here. If he requires that his place of residence should not be here, if he needs the allowance he should get it; if he wants to live in some other place because of his health-or it may be a matter of sentiment; since he cannot work any more, or because he wants to spend his old age in the place of his childhood -is there any reason why sentiment of that kind should be penalized? I suppose almost everybody in this house could see some reason for anyone wanting to do that if he were able to do so. We say he must live in Canada, where the eagle eyes of the means tester can look down the back of his neck all the time to see that he does not earn one more nickel than the act allows. I do not think that is dignified treatment for a veteran. If he can qualify in all respects, then his place of residence should not be a deterrent to his receiving the war veterans allowance. At the present time he may live here, he may qualify, he may get the allowance. Then, after two or three years he
may feel that he would like to move out, but the moment he crosses the border and enters a foreign country he ceases to be entitled to that war veterans allowance. I know it does not say so exactly in the act, but if there is any dispute about that I can quote from a letter I received from the pension commission pointing out that that is the case in one particular instance to which I drew their attention.
Another thing I want to mention is this. The war veterans allowance is not payable to the married veteran and his wife as having married status if they live apart. This again is very unfair and undignified). The man is, of course, the breadwinner. He is the one who should provide for his family, and as long as he is working and is able to provide for them we expect him to look after his wife and children. That is proper and we have a1 right to expect it. But the moment something happens to him and he is no longer able to support them, possibly because of inability to work, though he and his wife may have spent forty years together, they find it necessary now to split up, one living with one married child, with whom there is room, the other living with another. The moment they are split up because of their financial condition, the veteran ceases to be entitled to war veterans allowance except under single status.
That, Mr. Speaker,, is unfair. The allowance should be generous enough, the administration should be generous enough and the whole spirit of the act should be generous enough to say to the veteran: We should like both you and your lifelong spouse to be able to spend your remaining years together if you so desire, and therefore we will make it possible for you to do so.
I know it will be said there are a few veterans who are so cantankerous that their wives cannot live with them, and I think it may be said there are some men who are not veterans who are also so cantankerous that hardly anyone can get along with them. There may be exceptional cases, but in the main I believe the veterans want to continue their married status. They do not want to split up. When, however, they have to separate because of poor financial conditions they should not be deprived of the veterans allowance. I do not think they should be deprived of it merely because they have decided that it is necessary for them to separate under those circumstances.
There are a number of other criticisms that I should like to offer, but I do not want to take up too much time, because the matter is going to the committee and no doubt others will deal with them. On the points I have presented tonight to the house and to the
War Veterans Allowance Act

minister I would ask that serious and sympathetic consideration be given, because I believe that every single one of them is justifiable, every single one of them is possible, every single one of them will do a great deal to bring a measure of happiness and contentment to the few individuals in the class we are speaking of who are still left, and it will give some sense of security to some of the veterans of this war who some day will have to face the same condition as some of our older veterans have to put up with.

A certain young man was in the army and there was a fire. He was a very delicate fellow-I knew him well-and he went to the fire, worked there, and contracted a cold which turned into pneumonia. He fell dangerously ill. He received the last rites of the church, and after that some officers came to him and said, "You must sign a paper so that your mother will have a pension." He was very sick. I do not know whether they held his hand, but the paper was signed. It was a resignation from the army, and instead of giving an opportunity to his widowed mother to get a pension it deprived her of all pension. He died a day or two afterwards.
It was an abomination, and the men who did that should have been whipped. The mother applied for pension and got nothing. Finally I brought the case before the predecessor of the present minister and he decided to give an allowance of $40 a month to the mother. It is a pitiful case where the pension commission has been more stupid than ever, where officers have behaved very badly, shamefully, and where an allowance was some kind of help to that widow.
This is a fact and I could mention many facts like it. The trouble we have now with the pension commission is that they never give the benefit of the doubt to the returned man. I have within my knowledge cases of men who have been declared fit, who have been accepted in the army and who have served for a long time. I have in mind the case of one man who was on guard duty at the forts at Levis. He was outside, and had no place to warm himself when it was cold, when the wind was blowing fiercely in the winter and when there were snowstorms. He lost his health. I asked for a pension. I was told that his illness was anterior to his enlistment How is it that some of the medical corps were accepting these soldiers into the army as fit? They served well. They followed the orders they received. Yet after they had served for some years they were not entitled to any pension and got nothing at all. I obtained no allowance for that man. He lost his health; yet he had nothing at all. His illness or his disability was said to be anterior to his enlistment.
All those doctors should be crucified. I have said on many an occasion that a large number of medical doctors were the scum of the medical profession. I received letters of protest, and to those who were protesting I sent the

He said, "Well it is very sad." It was sad and unfortunate, but nobody was punished.
I have another case, that of a widow who has been deprived of a pension. This is a Toronto case, where a man was suffering from acute appendicitis. The doctor gave him a strong purgative and the poor boy died. The doctor was a murderer.
