speechtext:
We in this group, Mr. Speaker, are glad that the government have seen fit to bring down this bill amending the War Veterans Allowance Act, if for no other purpose than to have it thoroughly discussed in the veterans affairs committee so that the various veterans organizations can make representations regarding it. Amendments to this act are long overdue, but I am afraid that the proposals contained in this bill fall far short of those required to deal adequately with the situation. When the minister spoke he paid a fine tribute to the old veterans, and one that was well deserved. However, after listening to the minister, it is hard for me to understand how the government can bring down a bill of this kind and consider that they are doing justice to the returned men.
The War Veterans Allowance Act was first introduced in 1930. It made an allowance of S20 a month available at the age of sixty to the veteran who was permanently unemployable and who had served in a theatre of actual warfare. It has often been said that the act was recognition of the fact that a veteran had pre-aged by ten years and that, therefore, the old age pension was being made available to him at sixty years of age instead of seventy. I think it is well to keep in mind that fact and to note that at the present time the amount of the old age pension is in excess of the amount of the war veterans allowance. Later on the age limit was reduced below sixty years where the veteran was unable to maintain himself because of disability; some classes of widows were introduced and the amount of the allowance was increased to $30 a month.
The foregoing short summary, I think, goes to show that the war veterans allowance may be considered as the veteran's last resort. When he is unable to get a disability pension because of some technicality in the act or is, on the other hand, too old to work, he can apply for the war veterans allowance; and all he can get under the act is $30 a month. The same is true for the non-pensioned widow. I think all hon. members will agree that $30 a month today is not a living allowance. All that $30 a month does is to permit a veteran to struggle for an existence. As I have already said, he is not as well off as the old age pensioner. The new bill does not propose to increase the amount of the allowance. It merely provides for a supplementary allowance that may be paid in case of need, if need can be shown. Then the increase is limited to $10 a month for both single and married veterans. The new bill
War Veterans Allowance Act

also increases the amount of permissible income from $125 to $250 for single veterans and from $250 to $375 for married persons. But it cancels the provision for $125 casual earnings. Therefore it is true that the bill does bring about some improvement in the act. On the other hand, that improvement falls far short of what is required to deal adequately with the situation. The Canadian Legion and the Canadian council of veterans associations have asked that the allowances be increased to $50 for a single veteran and to $100 for a married man. That is to say, the national council of veterans associations has asked that the allowance for a married veteran be increased to $100, while the legion has suggested that it be increased to at least $85.
I know the question will immediately be raised as to whether or not the country can afford allowances of this size. Well, whenever that question is raised my mind always goes back to the veterans committee of 1936, when we were considering both the war veterans allowance and the matter of pensions. We were told by the minister of the day that unfortunately it was not so much a question of what the veterans should have but rather a question of what the country could afford; and he went on to say that the country was bankrupt. It may be true that the country was bankrupt at that time, because we were suffering under the financial policies of Hon. Charles Dunning, which in itself was enough to bankrupt any country. But that is not the situation today. Today conditions are far different from 1936. I noticed that the Canadian Press quoted the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) as saying on April 2 that Canada is enjoying a boom of unprecedented proportions, even though the people do not seem to be aware of it. Well, if the minister is aware of it that is something. It is only natural that the people would not appreciate it when they see veterans having to subsist on a miserable pittance of $30 a month, and old age pensioners receiving only $30 a month as far as the federal government is concerned. However, when we consider that today the national income is around $13 billion as compared with $4 billion in 1936 no one can argue, as it was argued in 1936, that we cannot afford to deal adequately with the veterans of this country.
The government have talked a great deal about our moral, obligation to look after people in foreign countries, and we in this house have voted hundreds of millions of dollars to help those people. I should say the first obligation of this country is to look after those men who fought and made victory possible, and that should be considered a first charge against

the national income before consideration is given to the needs of people in other countries. After all, there is an old saying that charity should begin at home. Well, veterans are not
asking for charity. They are merely asking for fair compensation for themselves and their dependents for services already rendered. I think it is time the government put an end to the hypocritical .paying of lip service to these men, and instead dealt honestly, fairly and squarely with them.
I want to give just one example of the type of niggardly assistance being given to veterans under this act; and mind you, Mr. Speaker, when I say this I am not for a moment criticizing the administration of the act. My experience has been that the people administering this act go just as far as the act permits; but that is all they can do. I know of a case right here in the city of Ottawa, of a veteran who has reached the age of seventy-nine years, while his wife is well over seventy. He was awarded a full pension of $60 a month for the two of them; but that was reduced to $38 a month because the veteran found he could not live on $60 and managed to get a few hours work a day which brought him in $10 a week. So his pension was reduced. He was paying $45 a month in rent. It was suggested by the investigator that perhaps he should find cheaper accommodation, but the investigator frankly admitted that she did not know where he would be able to get another apartment at that or any other price. If it is to be argued that a veteran is paying too much rent for the apartment in which he lives, then I think those administering the war veterans allowance will have to accept the responsibility of finding him cheaper accommodation. As long as he has to pay that rent that must be recognized as one of the expenses he has to meet. In view of the fact that this veteran's permissible income had been exceeded, he had to pay back a certain amount of money. I am glad to say that, instead of stopping his allowance entirely, the administration deducted $3 a month in order to make up the amount he had been overpaid, which of course further reduced his pension to $35 a month. The point I want to make is that this veteran is seventy-nine years of age and his wife is over seventy. He never applied for any assistance until he was seventy-seven; yet they had to check up and by the act they were forced to reduce the amount of his allowance in view of the fact that he was exceeding his permissible income. I believe that this question of the permissible income is something that should be carefully investigated. In my opinion that permissible income should be

War Veterans Allowance Act
increased to a figure which would make it possible for a veteran to live in a city where rents may be higher than in certain other parts of the country.
We of this group believe that the War Veterans Allowance Act should be amended to provide for the following changes. We believe that there should be an increase in the allowances to $50 a month for a single veteran and to $100 for a married couple. We believe that the means test should be eliminated:; or, if the government cannot see its way clear to go that far, that at least the permissible income plus the allowance should be equal to the amount of income tax exemption, which at the presenttime would be around 81,500 for a married veteran. We believe that, for the purposes of this act, England should be considered a theatre of actual warfare in regard to world war I; that already is the case with respect to world war II. As far as world war I is concerned), a veteran who got only to England is not eligible for a war veterans allowance. When we remember that many of those veterans who enlisted for overseas service and got to England were only too anxious to go farther but were not allowed to do so, it does not seem fair that at this stage of the game they should be barred from the benefits of the war veterans allowance purely for that reason. Furthermore we believe that the benefits of the act should be made available to persons who served during world war I as a member of His Majesty's imperial forces, whether or not he was domiciled in Canada just prior to the outbreak of war. I have had cases of veterans who had been domiciled in Canada for a number of years prior to the war but who went to England perhaps two or three months before war broke out. I had one case of a veteran who went overseas because of the illness of his father. It was ruled that this man was not domiciled in this country because he was in England at the time war was declared, and as a result he has been denied the benefits of the War Veterans Allowance Act.
These are matters which we believe should be thoroughly discussed in the committee, and we are hoping that when this bill goes to the veterans committee some of the changes we have suggested may be brought about. Most of the suggestions I have outlined I think were also made by hon. members speaking for the C.C.F. party and the Progressive Conservative party. As a matter of fact they are suggestions that have been made for a number of years by the various veteran organizations in this country. If the government are really sincere in their desire to see that the old veteran gets a
square deal, then they should find ways and means of making these suggestions a reality. As the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) has stated, this bill it to be referred to the veterans committee, of which I am a member. Therefore I shall not say anything more at this time but will reserve any further remarks until the legislation, is considered by that committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister said when he was introducing the bill, the benefits of the War Veterans Allowance Act applied principally to the veterans of world war I. There are a few recipients of allowances who served in previous wars, such as the northwest field force and the South African war. There are a limited number of veterans who served in world war II and who are eligible for the allowance. In the main, however, they are men of the first world war.
I should like to call attention to the spirit of those times, the conditions which existed in 1914. That was the first citizen army war in more than a hundred years. It had been over a hundred years since the Canadian citizen had taken up arms in the defence of his country. When 1914 came there was a rush of men to join the various regiments, and they proceeded overseas. There was very little information upon which to build veterans rehabilitation schemes when the war came to an end.
In this connection I would quote the remarks of the present deputy minister of veterans affairs in a speech he made in 1943, which I think indicates the rush that existed for men to get discharged from that war. He states:
The principal problem at the conclusion of the first world war was in the fact that Canada, with a population of about 8,000,000 at that time, had to fit back into civilian life approximately 423,000 men within less than a year. All wished to return to civilian life as quickly as possible.
I would emphasize the words: "all wished to return to civilian life as quickly as possible." The men of those years were not pension conscious. A great many men who perhaps had received some small disability, either by war wounds or exposure in the trenches, were anxious to get back into civilian life. They did not bother about declaring their disability. As time went on, those disabilities, not being declared, began to weigh more heavily on the men. And as the years advanced, the men became more and more dependent upon any pension or any allowance they might receive.
This war veterans allowance is really a form of retirement scheme for ex-servicemen who have fulfilled service conditions. I suggest that in a way it is really a contributory retirement
War Veterans Allowance Act

scheme, because the men made their contribution in service in the trenches, instead of making it as a monetary contribution, as they might have done had they stayed at home.
As I have said, the cost of living has gone up since those days. Men have become more and more dependent upon whatever allowance or pension they may receive from a pension scheme or by way of allowance.
Listening to the build-up given, and justly so, by the minister to the services rendered by these men, I could not help repeating the words of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) when he said that Bill No. 196 is most disappointing. It has certainly not gone as far as the veterans had hoped it would go, nowhere near as far. It is disappointing in many respects. And I think it is particularly disappointing after the encouraging statements made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in New York a week ago, as reported by the Canadian Press. After describing what a prosperous state Canada was in and how we were experiencing boom conditions, he went on to say that in a few weeks time he would be reporting to parliament in his budget speech, and that he would be able to declare a surplus which would bring a glow to the heart of any Canadian finance minister. I suggest that the puny increases authorized or suggested in this bill will not bring much of a glow to the hearts of those old soldiers who will receive only this pittance. There is no warmth in this bill to bring a glow, even to the tips of their fingers.
It seems to me that the principle upon which the framers of these amendments have worked is to give the smallest amount possible to the fewest number of men. The increases in the allowances are referred to as a supplementary allowance of $120 a year, or $10 a month, which may be allocated to a recipient at the discretion of the board. It is not automatic, but the board will decide whether that amount of $10 a month, or a lesser amount, is to be given to the veterans. The increase is not automatic; that has been declared by the minister in the house.
I suggest that, unlike the Pension Act where we were told that the cheques were ready for issue before Easter, there are no cheques ready for issue in connection with this measure. Those who will hope to get increases will have to have their cases reviewed by the board, and the decisions will be made no doubt in accordance with the regulations as hinted by the minister in his opening remarks. Certain regulations will be laid down for the guidance of the board; but a discretion will be left with

the board as to how much they will increase the allowance or allow by way of a supplementary allowance. I suggest that is all going to take time. These various cases will have to be reviewed. Time will be required and additional staff will be needed to look after all these cases.
Mention has been made of the permissible income. The impression was given, I thought, that there had been some increase in the permissible income. That is the amount of money that man may receive in addition to his allowance. The amount of money he may earn was classified under different headings, such as casual earnings for a single man of $125 a year, other income for a single man of $125 per annum and then unearned income of $25 per annum.	,
The former minister of veterans affairs informed me last year that the term "other income" was interpreted by the war veterans allowance board to mean income derived from any source; that is, investment, pension, superannuation, insurance payments, rentals, et cetera, or as a result of earnings as a gardener, plumber, carpenter or as any other type of artisan.	:
What has happened, and I think there is some reason to think there has been some improvement, is that casual earnings and other income have been amalgamated, making a permissible income other than allowance for a single man of $250 per annum. That is not a large amount to go out and earn. A man is hardly encouraged to go out and earn that extra amount. I would call your attention Mr. Speaker, to the fact that pensions are included in permissible income.
There has been an increase in pensions. A recipient of a war veterans allowance might have an 18 per cent disability pension. Under the old rates he would draw $11.25 a month in pension; his allowance, allowing for the [DOT] pension he was authorized to receive, would be $29.58 a month, making a total of $40.83 a month. Under the new rates of pension which are increased by 16 per cent, he would receive $13.05 a month, but his allowance would be reduced by virtue of the fact that the pension has gone up. My interpretation of the act is-I hope the minister will correct me if I am wrong-that with the new pension rate the allowance would be only $27.78 a month, still making a total of $40.83 a month.
While there has been an increase in one case, there has been a decrease in the other. The war veterans allowance recipient has gained through the increase in his pension, but he has lost in connection with his allowance.

I think that ought to be corrected, because that is hardly what was expected by the veterans when they were hoping to get an increase in their allowances.
I have some other remarks to make in connection with the failure to extend the benefits of this act to other groups of veterans, but I am afraid I cannot get through in the two minutes still left before eleven o'clock, so that I should like to move the adjournment of the debate.
